data.text/markdown:
Week 6 · Advanced DeFi

Last week you saw how a basic automated market maker (AMM) works: a pool holds two tokens, prices follow ||(x \cdot y = k||), and liquidity providers (LPs) earn fees for taking on impermanent loss. This week looks at what happens once real money and real adversaries show up:
  1. Uniswap v3 and v4. How concentrated liquidity makes LP capital work harder, and what that costs.
  2. DeFi governance. How token holders control a protocol, and how that control gets attacked.
  3. MEV (maximal extractable value). Who decides the order of transactions in a block, and how they profit from it.
How to use this notebook. Read top to bottom. Each interactive section starts with a short Try this box telling you what to change and what to look for. Sliders and dropdowns update everything below them instantly, and nothing you do here touches a real blockchain. The code is hidden; open a cell's menu if you want to see how something is calculated. Expect about 75–90 minutes for the lesson. The homework section at the end is separate.

data.text/html:
By the end of this week you should be able to:
  • Explain why Uniswap v2 wastes LP capital and how concentrated liquidity fixes it.
  • Calculate the capital efficiency of a v3 position and the token amounts it needs.
  • Convert between prices and ticks, and explain what happens when a swap crosses a tick.
  • Explain why a narrower range increases impermanent loss, and when a position becomes a range order.
  • Describe what Uniswap v4 changes: hooks, the singleton pool manager and flash accounting.
  • Walk through a governance proposal from submission to execution, and name the defences against flash-loan voting attacks.
  • Define MEV and explain front-running, back-running, sandwich attacks, JIT liquidity and arbitrage with a worked example.
  • Describe how transaction ordering moved from miners and gas auctions to today's proposer–builder separation.
  • Argue which kinds of MEV harm users and which ones keep markets working.
Term Meaning
AMM A smart contract that trades against a pool of two tokens using a pricing formula instead of an order book.
LP (liquidity provider) Someone who deposits both tokens into a pool and earns a share of trading fees.
Impermanent loss (IL) How much less an LP position is worth than just holding the tokens you deposited, caused by the pool rebalancing as the price moves.
Slippage The gap between the price you were quoted and the price you actually get. You set a slippage tolerance: the worst price you'll accept before the trade cancels (reverts).
Mempool The waiting room of transactions that have been broadcast but not yet included in a block. Anyone running a node can read it.
Validator / proposer Since Ethereum's switch to proof of stake in September 2022, validators (not miners) take turns proposing blocks.
Flash loan A loan with no collateral that must be borrowed and repaid in the same transaction. If it isn't repaid, the whole transaction reverts.

data.text/markdown:
Advanced DeFi Protocols

Uniswap v3

Uniswap v2, and the many forks that copied it, have a serious problem: they are not capital efficient. A v2 LP's deposit is spread along the whole ||(x \cdot y = k||) curve, so the pool has liquidity at every price from 0 to infinity. But prices spend almost all their time in a narrow band. In an ETH/USDC pool, the liquidity reserved for "ETH trades at $5" or "ETH trades at $5,000,000" sits idle and earns nothing, while it still exposes the LP to impermanent loss. Fees earned on the small slice that is used often don't make up for that loss. Uniswap v3 (launched May 2021) asked: can LPs put their liquidity only where trading actually happens, while the pool still has enough liquidity to cover any trade?

Concentrated liquidity

In v3 an LP picks a price range ||([p_a, p_b]||) and their liquidity is only used while the pool price is inside it. Different LPs pick different ranges, and one pool combines all of them, so the pool's total liquidity at each price is the sum of every position that covers that price. Each position is a separate record with its own range. In v3 that record is an NFT, because no two positions are interchangeable the way v2's LP tokens were. Example (from Uniswap's v3 launch post). ETH trades at 1,500 DAI.
  • Alice puts $1M into the full range, like v2: 333.33 ETH and 500,000 DAI.
  • Bob concentrates between 1,000 and 2,250 DAI. To get the same liquidity as Alice inside that range he only needs about $183.5k (61.19 ETH and 91,780 DAI).
While ETH stays between 1,000 and 2,250 DAI, Alice and Bob earn the same fees, even though Alice committed about 5.45× as much money. Bob can do something else with the other ~$816k. If ETH leaves his range, Bob earns nothing until it comes back. The fee rate is the same for everyone in a pool (0.3% of the trade, for example). Bob doesn't pay or charge a higher rate; he earns more per dollar deposited because each of his dollars supplies more liquidity while the price is in range.

data.text/html: Check the numbers yourself. Change Bob's range and see how much capital he needs to match Alice's liquidity at a price of 1,500.

An earlier version of this lesson used a range of 1,000–2,500, said Bob needs $183.5k, and got 6.3× by dividing "115.5 sqrt-price units" by ||(\sqrt{2500} - \sqrt{1000} = 18.38||). Three things go wrong:
  1. The numbers don't match each other. $183.5k is Uniswap's figure for a 1,000–2,250 range. For 1,000–2,500 Bob would need about $204k, an efficiency of 4.89×. Pick "2,500" above to see this.
  2. There is no "full range width" of 115.5. A full-range position covers ||(\sqrt{p}||) from 0 to infinity. You can't compare widths in sqrt-price space when one width is infinite.
  3. Efficiency depends on the current price, not just the range width. The correct formula compares how much each position is worth at the same liquidity ||(L||), at today's price ||(P||):
||[\text{capital efficiency} = \frac{2\sqrt{P}}{2\sqrt{P} - \sqrt{p_a} - P/\sqrt{p_b}}||]With ||(P = 1500||), ||(p_a = 1000||), ||(p_b = 2250||): ||(\frac{77.46}{77.46 - 31.62 - 31.62} = 5.45||). The derivation is in Real and virtual reserves below.

data.text/markdown:
Ticks and visualizing concentrated liquidity

v3 can't track every possible price range, so it splits the price line into discrete steps called ticks. Tick number ||(i||) (any integer, positive or negative) sits at price ||[p(i) = 1.0001^{\,i}||]So each tick is 0.01% (one basis point) away from its neighbour. The contract actually stores ||(\sqrt{p}||), so you will often see this written as ||(\sqrt{p(i)} = 1.0001^{\,i/2}||). That is the square root of the price, not the price itself. (An older version of this lesson mixed these two up.) Why store ||(\sqrt{p}||)? Inside a single range the amount of each token moves linearly in ||(\sqrt{p}||): ||(\Delta y = L\,\Delta\sqrt{p}||) and ||(\Delta x = L\,\Delta(1/\sqrt{p})||). That keeps swap math cheap. Position boundaries can't sit on any tick. Each fee tier has a tick spacing, and ranges have to start and end on multiples of it. Wider spacing means fewer ticks to cross during a swap, which saves gas.
Fee tier Tick spacing Smallest possible range width
0.01% 1 ≈ 0.01%
0.05% 10 ≈ 0.1%
0.30% 60 ≈ 0.6%
1.00% 200 ≈ 2%
Think of the space between two usable ticks as a bucket. The height of each bucket is how much liquidity sits in it. In v2 every bucket would be the same height, because every LP covers every price. In v3 the heights are uneven: tall near the current price, where LPs crowd in, and short far away.

  • With tick spacing 60, the nearest usable boundaries are tick 80,040 (price 2,991.7083) and tick 80,100 (price 3,009.7116).
  • That smallest bucket is 0.60% wide.

data.text/markdown:
Providing liquidity in Uniswap v3

When you open a position you choose two ticks, and the range decides what mix of tokens you deposit, not the price alone.
  • Buckets entirely above the current price hold only ETH. The price only gets there if traders buy ETH, so those buckets need ETH to hand out.
  • Buckets entirely below the current price hold only USDC, ready to buy ETH from sellers if the price falls.
  • Only the bucket containing the current price holds a mix.
So the ratio you deposit isn't 50/50 like v2. A range sitting mostly above today's price needs mostly ETH; a range mostly below needs mostly USDC. As the price drops toward your lower bound, your position fills up with ETH. As it rises toward your upper bound, it fills up with USDC. The explorer below puts this together. It is this week's main explorable model.

Pick a price range, then move \"ETH price later\" to see what your position is worth.\u003c/span\u003e\n\u003col\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003ePredict first:\u003c/strong\u003e if you narrow the range to 2,900–3,100, will a 10% price move hurt you more or less than with the default range?\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eNarrow the range and watch \u003cem\u003ecapital efficiency\u003c/em\u003e climb. Then move the later price to 3,300 and compare impermanent loss for your range with a full-range position.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eDrag the later price outside your range. Check the token mix: you now hold only one token, and you stop earning fees.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003ePut the whole range above 3,000 (say 3,200–3,600). You deposit only ETH. That is a \u003cstrong\u003erange order\u003c/strong\u003e, covered further down.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ol\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"info"'></marimo-callout-output>

Reading the result. You deposit 1.667 ETH + 5,000 USDC ($10,000 at 3,000). At a later price of 3,300 the position holds 0.932 ETH + 7,312 USDC. Compared with just holding what you deposited, your range has an impermanent loss of -1.07%. A full-range position would have lost -0.11% over the same move. Narrower ranges lose more because the pool sells your rising token (and buys the falling one) faster over a short stretch of price. Notice the ratio. Your IL is about 9.5× the full-range IL, and your fees are 9.5× too. That's not a coincidence: inside the range, a concentrated position loses exactly what a full-range position with the same liquidity L would lose. Fees and IL scale up together, so while you're in range, concentrating makes a profitable position more profitable and a losing one lose faster. Range width starts to really hurt once the price leaves the range: fees stop, and IL keeps growing.

• One position against a constant price path. We only compare the start and the end. Real fee income depends on how much trading happens while the price is in your range, which the model doesn't simulate.
  • Fees aren't included in the IL numbers. The "break even" line tells you how much fee income you'd need; whether you actually earn it depends on volume.
  • No tick rounding. Real ranges snap to the fee tier's tick spacing (see the tick calculator above); the difference is under 2%.
  • No gas costs. Opening, closing and re-centring a position each costs a transaction.
  • Ignores other LPs. Your actual fee share depends on how much liquidity others have in the same buckets.

data.text/markdown:
Swapping with Uniswap v3

Inside one bucket, a v3 pool behaves exactly like a v2 pool with that bucket's liquidity: price moves along an ||(x \cdot y = k||) curve. When a trade uses up a bucket, the pool crosses a tick: it updates its active liquidity to the next bucket's value and keeps filling the trade there. "Uses up" is literal. Say you're buying ETH. As the price rises through a bucket, the bucket hands out its ETH and fills with USDC. When it runs out of ETH it can't sell any more, so the trade moves into the next bucket up. That bucket is still full of ETH, becomes the active one, and starts taking USDC. Deep buckets (tall bars) absorb a lot of USDC with little price movement. Shallow buckets let the price jump. Try a large trade below and watch it chew through several buckets.

data.text/markdown:
Real and virtual reserves

How do we describe a concentrated position with a curve we already understand? A position only holds tokens inside ||([p_a, p_b]||). Imagine instead that it were a normal v2 position, with liquidity everywhere. Its reserves on that imaginary curve are called virtual reserves ||((x_v, y_v)||). They satisfy the usual ||[x_v \cdot y_v = L^2, \qquad P = \frac{y_v}{x_v}||]where ||(L||) is the position's liquidity (so ||(L^2||) plays the role of ||(k||)), and prices are always "USDC per ETH", i.e. ||(y||) per ||(x||). Solving those two equations gives the virtual reserves at any price: ||[x_v = \frac{L}{\sqrt{P}}, \qquad y_v = L\sqrt{P}||]The real reserves ||((x, y)||) are what the position actually holds. The trick is that a concentrated position only needs to hold enough to get from the current price to the edge of its range:
  • At the top, ||(P = p_b||), it has sold all its ETH, so ||(x = 0||) while ||(x_v = L/\sqrt{p_b}||).
  • At the bottom, ||(P = p_a||), it has spent all its USDC, so ||(y = 0||) while ||(y_v = L\sqrt{p_a}||).
The real reserves are the virtual reserves minus the part that's never needed: ||[x = \frac{L}{\sqrt{P}} - \frac{L}{\sqrt{p_b}}, \qquad y = L\sqrt{P} - L\sqrt{p_a}||]Rearranging gives the curve for real reserves (whitepaper eq. 2.2): ||[\left(x + \frac{L}{\sqrt{p_b}}\right)\left(y + L\sqrt{p_a}\right) = L^2||]Note that the real reserves do not satisfy ||(x \cdot y = L^2||). Only the virtual ones do. That's the shift: the real curve is the v2 curve slid toward the origin until it touches both axes at ||(p_a||) and ||(p_b||). Where capital efficiency comes from. A full-range position at price ||(P||) is worth ||(x_v P + y_v = 2L\sqrt{P}||). A concentrated one is worth ||(xP + y = L\left(2\sqrt{P} - \sqrt{p_a} - P/\sqrt{p_b}\right)||). Same ||(L||), smaller deposit. The ratio of the two is the capital efficiency formula from the Alice and Bob example.

Concentrated liquidity as a limit order

What happens when the price leaves your range? Your position turns entirely into one token. Say you provide liquidity in the ETH/USDC pool between 2,000 and 2,200 USDC:
  • If ETH rises above 2,200, the pool has sold all your ETH on the way up. You hold only USDC.
  • If ETH falls below 2,000, the pool has spent all your USDC buying ETH on the way down. You hold only ETH.
This is what keeps liquidity constant in ||(\sqrt{p}||) space and only active inside your range. It also means LPs can use v3 as a kind of limit order, called a range order: put a narrow range entirely above the current price, deposit only ETH, and if the price rises through it your ETH is sold for USDC. Example. DAI trades just below 1.001 USDC and you want to sell 1M DAI. You open a position on the DAI/USDC pool from 1.001 to 1.002 USDC. That is entirely above the current price, so you deposit only DAI. If DAI rises through the range, your DAI is gradually swapped for USDC, and once it's above 1.002 you hold only USDC, plus the fees you earned along the way. Withdraw then, or a fall back through the range will swap you back into DAI. A correction on impermanent loss. An older version of this lesson said this behaviour minimizes impermanent loss. It doesn't. Once you're out of range the pool stops rebalancing you, but that's because you've already been fully converted into the token that did worse. If ETH keeps rising, your all-USDC position falls further behind simply holding. In the explorer, move the later price far above your range and watch the IL keep growing. A narrower range reaches that point after a smaller price move. Concentrated liquidity amplifies impermanent loss per dollar; it doesn't reduce it. You're paid for this with higher fees while in range.

data.text/markdown:
Observations

  • Uniswap v3 is a hybrid of an AMM and an order book. Each LP effectively posts liquidity at a chosen set of prices, like orders on a book, but trades still execute against a formula, with no matching engine.
  • Fee tiers. Each token pair can have one pool per fee tier, and LPs choose which pool to join. v3 launched in May 2021 with 0.05%, 0.30% and 1%. Uniswap governance added a 0.01% tier in late 2021, aimed at stablecoin pairs. Those four are the defaults on Ethereum mainnet, but the factory contract lets governance enable more, so "v3 has three (or four) fee tiers" is a statement about defaults, not a rule. In v4 a pool can use any fee, including a dynamic fee that a hook changes trade by trade. Lower fee tiers suit pairs that barely move against each other (USDC/USDT): LPs there take little impermanent loss and compete on price. Volatile or obscure pairs need higher fees to compensate LPs.
  • Active management costs time and gas. A concentrated position only earns while in range, so LPs who want to stay in range must withdraw and re-deposit, which costs a few transactions each time. Earlier versions of this lesson blamed this on positions being NFTs; the NFT is just the receipt. The real cost is the repeated transactions and the attention needed. On Ethereum mainnet that gas has historically priced small LPs out of active management. On layer-2 networks, where v3 and v4 are also deployed, it's far cheaper, and automated "liquidity manager" vaults now rebalance positions for depositors in exchange for a fee.
  • Sophisticated LPs earn more. Studies of v3 found that a large share of fees goes to a small group of professional LPs, and that many passive LPs would have been better off holding. (Loesch et al., 2021, is a widely cited early example; see Sources.)

Uniswap v4

Uniswap v4 went live on Ethereum mainnet and several other chains in January 2025. It keeps v3's concentrated-liquidity math and changes what a pool can do and how it's stored. Hooks. A pool can be attached to a hook, an external contract that Uniswap calls at fixed points: before and after a pool is initialized, liquidity is added or removed, a swap happens, or tokens are donated to LPs. Hooks let developers customize pool behaviour without forking Uniswap. Examples:
  • Dynamic fees: raise the fee when the market is volatile and lower it when it's calm.
  • Limit orders: fill and remove a range order automatically when the price crosses it.
  • Time-weighted average market makers (TWAMM): spread a huge order over hours to reduce price impact.
  • MEV protection or LP rewards: for example, charge more to trades that look like arbitrage and pass the proceeds to LPs.
A hook is chosen when the pool is created and can't be swapped out afterwards. It's arbitrary code, so a pool's safety now depends on its hook as well as on Uniswap's own contracts. The singleton. In v2 and v3 each pool was its own contract. In v4 every pool lives inside one contract, the PoolManager. Creating a pool is just a state update rather than a contract deployment, which makes it far cheaper. Flash accounting. During a sequence of actions (say, a swap through three pools), v4 only tracks how much each party owes or is owed and settles the net amounts once at the end. Tokens don't move between pools in between. This uses transient storage, storage that is wiped at the end of the transaction, added to Ethereum in the Dencun upgrade (March 2024, EIP-1153). Multi-hop trades get cheaper. Native ETH. v4 pools can hold ETH directly instead of requiring the wrapped ERC-20 version (WETH), saving a wrap and unwrap step.

data.text/markdown:
DeFi Governance

In DeFi governance, people who hold a protocol's governance token can propose and vote on changes to how the protocol works: fee levels, which assets a lending market accepts, how the treasury spends money, contract upgrades. Many DeFi projects use token governance to spread ownership and decision-making beyond the founding team. The vote doesn't just express an opinion. In a fully onchain system the winning proposal contains the exact contract calls to run, and the governance contract executes them. Whoever controls enough votes controls the protocol, including its treasury.

Voting

The usual rule is one token, one vote. A holder can vote For, Against or Abstain. Abstaining counts toward quorum (the minimum turnout a vote needs to be valid) but doesn't affect the outcome. One token, one vote gives large holders ("whales") most of the power. Alternatives have been proposed, such as quadratic voting, where ||(n||) tokens give you ||(\sqrt{n}||) votes. It has a big weakness onchain: wallets are free, so a whale can split their tokens across many addresses and get the votes back. (Splitting 1,000,000 tokens into 100 wallets turns 1,000 votes into 100 × √10,000 = 10,000.) This is called a Sybil attack, and it's why quadratic voting usually needs some proof that each voter is a distinct person.

Proposals

Anyone holding (or delegated) more than a proposal threshold of voting power can submit a proposal. A typical onchain proposal goes through these steps:

data.text/html: <marimo-mermaid data-diagram='"\nflowchart LR\n    A[Proposal submitted\u003cbr/\u003eproposer meets threshold] --\u003e B[Voting delay\u003cbr/\u003evoting power snapshot taken]\n    B --\u003e C[Voting period\u003cbr/\u003eFor / Against / Abstain]\n    C --\u003e|quorum met and For \u003e Against| D[Queued in timelock\u003cbr/\u003ee.g. 2 days]\n    C --\u003e|fails| X[Defeated]\n    D --\u003e E[Executed\u003cbr/\u003econtract calls run]\n"'></marimo-mermaid>

data.text/markdown:
Each step is there for a reason. The snapshot at the start fixes everyone's voting power, so buying or borrowing tokens after a proposal goes up doesn't help. The timelock gives users who disagree with a passed proposal time to withdraw their money before it takes effect. Proposals come in many forms: parameter changes, treasury grants, contract upgrades and non-binding "temperature checks". Many DAOs also vote offchain first on Snapshot, where votes are free signed messages rather than transactions, then run a binding onchain vote or let a multisig carry out the result.

Delegation

Delegation lets you give another address the right to vote with your tokens' voting power, while you keep the tokens. In the most common token standard (OpenZeppelin's ERC20Votes, and Compound's COMP before it) tokens don't count for anything in votes until they're delegated, even if you delegate to yourself. Many governance tokens are held by early investors (often venture capital funds) and the founding team. Partly because it looks bad for a handful of funds to control a "decentralized" protocol, and partly because voting well takes time, many of them delegate tokens to active, independent delegates. Student blockchain groups including Blockchain at Berkeley have been delegates in protocols such as Uniswap and Compound. Delegation also has a downside: a few delegates can end up holding a large share of all active votes.

Governor contracts

Most Ethereum DAOs run their onchain votes through a Governor contract, which handles proposing, voting, the timelock and execution.
  • GovernorAlpha / GovernorBravo were written by Compound in 2020. Uniswap and many other early DAOs copied them, and they remain in use (historical but still relevant).
  • OpenZeppelin Governor (2021) is a modular version of the same idea. Voting rules, quorum, counting and timelock are pluggable pieces. It's the common starting point for new DAOs today.

Governance attack sandbox

In April 2022 (historical), an attacker drained roughly $182 million from the stablecoin protocol Beanstalk. They didn't exploit a bug. They borrowed about $1 billion in assets with flash loans, used them to get a two-thirds supermajority, passed a proposal that sent the protocol's funds to themselves, and repaid the loans, all in one transaction. Beanstalk counted voting power from current balances, and its emergency path let a proposal that had waited 24 hours execute immediately with a supermajority. The sandbox below is a fictional DAO with 100 million tokens. A malicious proposal tries to send the 15M-token treasury to the attacker. Everyone except the attacker votes Against, if they vote at all.

data.text/markdown:
Miner / Maximal Extractable Value

Fundamentals

Whoever builds a block decides which transactions go in and in what order. Before Ethereum moved to proof of stake (September 2022) that was miners, and the term was miner extractable value. Validators now propose blocks, so it's called maximal extractable value (MEV): the profit available to whoever controls transaction ordering. Two facts make MEV possible:
  1. Transactions wait in the public mempool before they're included, and anyone can read them.
  2. The block builder chooses the order. Nothing in the protocol forces first-come, first-served.

data.text/html: A transaction is a signed message, not an encrypted one. To be included it has to be broadcast to nodes, so its contents (which contract, which function, which amounts) are visible to anyone listening. The protocol only checks that each transaction in a block is valid; it doesn't care about the order. So the builder can put transactions in whatever order is most profitable for them, or add their own.

data.text/markdown:
Over time, block producers and the bots working with them realized that knowing what's about to happen in a block is very profitable. The basic moves:
Move What happens Example
Front-running Your transaction goes right before a target transaction. Buy a token before someone's big buy order pushes the price up.
Back-running Your transaction goes right after a target transaction. Arbitrage a price gap the target trade just created.
Sandwich attack One transaction before and one after the target. Buy before a victim's swap, sell right after it.
Censorship Leave a target transaction out. Since the U.S. sanctioned Tornado Cash (August 2022), some builders and relays exclude transactions touching sanctioned addresses.
Censoring a transaction normally means giving up its fee, so it's usually done for legal or political reasons rather than profit. (An earlier version of this lesson called it purely a "social attack"; since 2022 it's been a real policy question for Ethereum.)

AMM sandwich attacks

Every trade against an AMM moves the pool's price. A buy removes ETH from an ETH/USDC pool and adds USDC, so ETH gets more expensive.

data.text/html: The pool's price is just the ratio of its reserves, ||(P = y/x||). Any trade changes both reserves, so it changes the ratio. Trades that are large relative to the pool move it most: 100 ETH barely moves a pool holding 100,000 ETH, but moves a 1,000-ETH pool a lot. Concentrated liquidity matters here too: a pool with deep liquidity near the current price absorbs big trades with less movement.

data.text/markdown:
If you know a trade is about to push the price up, you can buy just before it and sell just after it for a profit. If a trade will push the price down, you can do the reverse: sell the asset first, or use a flash loan to borrow and sell it, then buy it back cheaper. A sandwich attack does this to a specific victim. The attacker sees a pending swap in the mempool and arranges three transactions in a row:
  1. Front-run: the attacker buys ETH, pushing the price up.
  2. Victim's trade: the victim buys ETH at the worse price.
  3. Back-run: the attacker sells the ETH they just bought at the higher price.
The attacker can only push the price so far. Every swap has a slippage tolerance, the minimum amount out the victim will accept. If the front-run is too big, the victim's trade reverts and the attacker is left holding ETH bought at a premium. So the victim's slippage tolerance is the attacker's budget. These days most sandwiches aren't run by block producers themselves but by independent bots called searchers, who pay builders to include their transactions in the right order (see Flashbots below). The simulator below runs real constant-product math. It also compares the different ways transaction ordering has worked on Ethereum.

Then try it.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eMake the pool much deeper (10,000+ ETH). Why does the attack become unprofitable?\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eLower the slippage tolerance until the attack stops paying for its gas.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eCompare the three ordering systems in the bar chart at the bottom. Which changes the \u003cem\u003evictim's\u003c/em\u003e outcome, and which only changes who gets the attacker's profit?\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ol\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"info"'></marimo-callout-output>

Same trade, three ways of ordering transactions

The bars split the value from this one trade between the victim, the searcher and whoever produces the block. Share bid away decides how much of the searcher's profit goes to the block producer. The victim's loss is bigger than the other two bars combined: the difference goes to the pool's LPs as trading fees on the attacker's two trades, and to gas.
  • Public mempool, gas auction (historical). Searchers fought by raising gas prices in public. Only one can win; the other 3 still paid gas for transactions that failed onchain (≈ $15 wasted here), and the bidding drove up gas for everyone else.
  • Public mempool via MEV-Boost (today). The victim loses the same amount. What changes is that searchers bid privately in sealed bundles, so losing bids cost nothing and don't clog the chain. The profit goes mostly to the builder and proposer instead of being burned as wasted gas.
  • Private RPC with refunds. The victim sends their trade to a private endpoint such as Flashbots Protect or MEV Blocker instead of the public mempool. Searchers can't see it in time to front-run it; they can only bid to back-run it, arbitraging the pool back to the market price. MEV Blocker pays 90% of that back-run's value to the user. Here that's a $604.14 refund instead of a $500.00 loss.

• One pool, constant product (Uniswap v2 math). A v3 pool behaves the same way inside one bucket; across buckets the numbers change but the logic doesn't.
  • The external ETH price stays at 3,000. The back-run in the private-RPC case trades the pool back to that price.
  • The attacker picks the largest front-run that keeps the victim's trade valid. In this model profit always rises with front-run size up to that limit; real attackers solve the same problem.
  • "Share bid away" is a single input. Real bids depend on how many searchers spot the same opportunity; competitive opportunities often see over 90% bid away.
  • The private-RPC case assumes the private endpoint keeps the trade private and that a searcher back-runs it. Smaller trades may get no back-run and therefore no refund.
  • The gas auction and MEV-Boost cases are shown with the same victim loss on purpose. They differ in where the money goes and in wasted block space, not in what the victim pays.

data.text/markdown:
Just-in-time (JIT) liquidity

LPs normally carry impermanent loss risk for as long as their liquidity sits in the pool. A JIT liquidity provider avoids almost all of it:
  1. They spot a large swap in the mempool.
  2. Right before it, they add a big concentrated position around the current price.
  3. The swap executes, mostly against their liquidity, and they collect most of the fee.
  4. Right after, they withdraw.
They hold the position for one block, so the price has no time to move against them beyond the swap itself. JIT is mostly seen on Uniswap v3, because concentrated liquidity lets a single position dominate the active bucket. The swapper isn't hurt (they get a better price thanks to the extra liquidity), but the pool's regular LPs lose most of that trade's fees.

Liquidation front-running

In lending protocols, whoever first calls liquidate on an undercollateralized loan collects the liquidation bonus. If a searcher sees someone else's liquidation transaction in the mempool, they can copy it and put theirs first, taking the bonus.

data.text/html: Back-run the oracle update. The loan isn't liquidatable until the new price is onchain, so a liquidation placed before the update would fail. Placed directly after it in the same block, the liquidation succeeds and the searcher is first in line for the bonus. This is why liquidations are such a competitive MEV category: everyone watches the same oracles.

data.text/markdown:
Arbitrage

Ordinary arbitrage reacts to prices after a trade has happened: someone notices one market is cheaper than another, then trades. If you can see a trade before it's included, you know exactly what price gap it will create, and you can place your arbitrage directly behind it in the same block (a back-run). The market is back in line by the end of the block. Worked example (from this lesson's slides). An ETH/USDC pool holds 4,500 ETH and 10,000,000 USDC, so ETH costs 10,000,000 ÷ 4,500 ≈ $2,222. Someone swaps 1,000,000 USDC for ETH (no fees, for simplicity). Now the pool holds 11,000,000 USDC and ||(45{,}000{,}000{,}000 \div 11{,}000{,}000 \approx 4{,}091||) ETH, so ETH costs about $2,689 in this pool. If ETH is still $2,222 elsewhere (say, on another chain or exchange), an arbitrageur buys ETH there and sells it into this pool until the two prices meet. The same numbers show how valuable it is to see that 1M swap coming: a searcher who buys before it and sells after it is running exactly the sandwich from the simulator.

Generalized front-running

Early MEV bots looked for specific patterns, like a big AMM trade to sandwich. Generalized front-runners don't need to understand the transaction at all:
  1. Take any pending transaction.
  2. Simulate it with the bot's own address as the sender.
  3. If the copy makes money, submit it with a higher priority fee so it lands first.
More advanced bots simulate internal calls too. Say you write a contract only you can call, which calls a lending protocol to perform a liquidation. Copying your outer transaction fails because only you can call your contract, but a smarter bot spots the inner liquidation call and makes it directly. The block builder often includes your original transaction as well, which now does nothing useful, and still collects your fee.

data.text/markdown:
Priority Gas Auctions

This section is mostly historical: it describes Ethereum before Flashbots (2020–21). The incentives it describes still matter. At first, only miners could reliably profit from transaction ordering, because only they controlled it. Then other people found they could steer where their transactions landed by bidding.

data.text/html: By fee per unit of gas, highest first. Block space is capped by the gas limit, so the producer wants the most fee per unit of space. Since EIP-1559 (August 2021) the base fee is burned, so the producer only keeps the priority fee (tip): sort by tip per gas. That's the default ordering in Ethereum clients, and exactly what gas auctions exploited.

data.text/markdown:
Because miners sorted by gas price, a bot that wanted to be right before a target transaction could broadcast with a slightly higher gas price, and one that wanted to be right after could try a slightly lower one (less reliable, since other transactions could slip between). The people running these bots came to be called searchers. When several searchers spotted the same opportunity, they bid against each other in the open, re-broadcasting with higher and higher gas prices within seconds. This was named a priority gas auction (PGA). Problems with PGAs
  • Wasted block space. Every losing bid still landed onchain as a failed or useless transaction that paid gas.
  • Gas spikes. Bidding wars pushed gas prices up for everyone. Ordinary users were priced out or overpaid.
  • Consensus risk. When one block's MEV is worth much more than the block reward, a miner is tempted to re-org the chain (re-mine a recent block) to capture it, which threatens finality.
You saw the first two in the simulator: the gas-auction scenario charges losing searchers for failed transactions.

Flashbots

Flashbots is a research and development organization focused on MEV. Its first major product, Flashbots Auction (launched January 2021, historical), moved the gas-auction bidding off the public chain:
  • Searchers send bundles, ordered lists of transactions that must execute together in exactly that order or not at all. A bundle can include other people's transactions from the mempool (that's how a sandwich bundle is built).
  • Each bundle carries a bid, paid to the block producer either through gas or a direct ETH transfer, and only if the bundle is included.
  • Miners ran a modified client (mev-geth) that merged the most profitable bundles into their blocks alongside normal mempool transactions.
  • Losing bundles never land onchain, so failed bids cost nothing.
Miners in that system could see the bundles they received; what stopped them from stealing a searcher's strategy was reputation and the risk of being cut off from future bundles. (An earlier version of this lesson said bundle contents were hidden from miners.) Flashbots reported that miners controlling the large majority of Ethereum's hash rate had joined by 2021. Flashbots also offered a way for ordinary users to send transactions privately, so that they never entered the public mempool. Today's version is Flashbots Protect.

After the Merge: proposer–builder separation

In proof of stake there are no miners. Ethereum's validators take turns proposing blocks, and most of them don't build their own. Since September 2022 the dominant setup has been MEV-Boost, open-source software from Flashbots that implements proposer–builder separation (PBS):

data.text/html: <marimo-mermaid data-diagram='"\nflowchart LR\n    U[Users] --\u003e|public mempool| S[Searchers]\n    U --\u003e|private RPC| B\n    S --\u003e|bundles + bids| B[Builders\u003cbr/\u003eassemble whole blocks]\n    B --\u003e|block + bid| R[Relays\u003cbr/\u003echeck blocks, hide contents]\n    R --\u003e|header + bid only| P[Proposer\u003cbr/\u003evalidator picks highest bid]\n    P --\u003e|signs header| R\n    R --\u003e|full block published| N[Ethereum]\n"'></marimo-mermaid>

data.text/markdown:
1. Searchers find opportunities and send bundles to builders.
  2. Builders combine bundles and ordinary transactions into the most valuable block they can, and bid for the right to have it proposed.
  3. Relays sit in the middle. They check that blocks are valid and pay what they promise, and they show the proposer only the block header and the bid, not the transactions.
  4. The proposer signs the header with the highest bid without seeing what's inside. Only then is the full block revealed. This commit-then-reveal step is what actually stops proposers from stealing MEV.
Effects. Anyone can now compete for MEV, not just block producers. Most MEV revenue ends up with validators, because builders bid against each other. Solo stakers earn about the same as large operators. When someone today says they're "doing MEV", they're most likely a searcher watching the mempool and sending bundles. New problems. MEV-Boost has been used for roughly 90% of Ethereum blocks in recent measurements (check relayscan.io for current numbers). A handful of builders produce most of those blocks, and a handful of relays carry them, which concentrates trust. Some builders and relays exclude transactions linked to sanctioned addresses. Ethereum researchers have proposed building PBS into the protocol itself, enshrined PBS (EIP-7732), to remove the reliance on relays; it's slated for a future network upgrade, so check its status before relying on it.

data.text/markdown:
Bad vs Good MEV?

For a long time MEV was simply seen as bad: it raised gas costs, gave users worse prices, destabilized the network and pushed users to bribe block producers. Most people now split it into two groups by who it affects. Usually harmful: sandwich attacks, oracle manipulation and liquidation front-running. They take value from a specific user or protocol and pass it to the searcher and block producer without improving anything. Often useful:
  • Arbitrage keeps prices consistent across markets. Without it, AMM prices would drift away from the real market. (The cost lands on LPs, who are the ones being arbitraged.)
  • Liquidations (including back-running an oracle update) close risky loans quickly, before they become bad debt.
  • JIT liquidity gives traders a better price, though it takes fees from regular LPs.
Some researchers argue that even sandwiching does useful work, by routing trades toward the deepest pools. It's a minority view, and in practice sandwiches mostly cost users who set loose slippage. Another response to MEV is to give it back to users: order-flow auctions like MEV Blocker and Flashbots' MEV-Share sell the right to back-run your transaction and refund most of the proceeds to you, as in the simulator. Sort each kind below and check your reasoning.

data.text/markdown:
Key takeaways

  • Concentrated liquidity trades range for efficiency. A narrower range gives more liquidity per dollar and more fees while in range, but it leaves the range sooner and takes larger impermanent loss over the same price move.
  • Capital efficiency depends on the current price and both bounds: ||(2\sqrt{P} / (2\sqrt{P} - \sqrt{p_a} - P/\sqrt{p_b})||). Uniswap's own example (1,000–2,250 at 1,500) gives about 5.45×.
  • Ticks are 0.01% price steps (||(p = 1.0001^i||)). Swaps move through buckets of liquidity and cross ticks when a bucket runs out.
  • Out of range, a position is entirely one token, the one that did worse. That makes range orders possible, and it's also why IL keeps growing.
  • Uniswap v4 adds programmability (hooks) and cheaper accounting (singleton, flash accounting), at the cost of trusting each pool's hook code.
  • Governance is only as strong as how voting power is measured. Snapshots stop flash loans, quorum and turnout stop cheap takeovers, and timelocks give users time to leave.
  • MEV comes from controlling transaction order. A sandwich attacker's budget is the victim's slippage tolerance.
  • Ordering moved from miners and public gas auctions to proposer–builder separation. That cut wasted gas and spread MEV to validators, but concentrated power in a few builders and relays.
  • Some MEV is a cost (sandwiches, copied liquidations); some keeps markets working (arbitrage, timely liquidations). Private RPCs and order-flow auctions let users avoid the first kind or get paid for the second.
